case_study_insert.main_stem: Zephyr Solar Roofing (ZSR) is a private limited company in the renewable construction products sector, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2018 by Sofia Zephyr, it designs recyclable-glass solar roof tiles for housebuilders and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. ZSR plans to invest $640,000 in a lamination line for recyclable-glass solar roof tiles with eco-packaging, financed by a $250,000 five-year bank loan, a $140,000 share issue and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $20.00 a unit and a selling price of $35.00, and currently produces 36,000 units a year. ZSR faces two problems: tile breakage is 3.1% and installation lead times are lengthening.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary, 2025: a survey of 450 homeowners found that 66% would choose solar roof tiles if installation were simpler and 61% would pay up to $2.00 more for recyclable-glass versions. Product returns for cracked tiles fell from 22 to 11 per 1,000. Average installation lead time is 9 days. The quality log records 3.1% breakage on standard tiles against 1.4% on the new laminated pilot. Records show 9 of 36 technicians trained on the laminator; the certification course costs $950 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Zephyr Solar Roofing for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base rate increased from 4.5% to 5.25%, raising finance costs. (2) The minimum wage rises 5.5% from $13.10 to $13.82 an hour from April 2026. (3) Glass and silicon input costs rose 11.3% year-on-year; eco-building inflation is 7.0% and residential retrofit spending grew 4.6%.

questions.question_text: ZSR used $250,000 retained profit toward its $640,000 lamination line. Explain two advantages for ZSR of retained profit over a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit needs no interest or repayments, protecting cash flow while ZSR carries fixed costs of $216,000 a year and a $250,000 five-year bank loan. The $250,000 can fund the recyclable-glass laminator immediately, helping reduce tile breakage from 3.1% toward the 1.4% pilot level without adding to debt.

Point 2: Internal funding leaves Sofia Zephyr's ownership undiluted and avoids pledging assets, so the $640,000 line is safe from repossession if retrofit demand slows. It also complements the $140,000 share issue by preserving cash for the 9-day installation lead time and for absorbing the 11.3% rise in glass and silicon costs, giving ZSR flexibility that an extra loan covenant would remove.

Retaining $250,000 also avoids new loan covenants while ZSR works to bring the 3.1% breakage down to the 1.4% pilot level, so the $640,000 line can approach its 36,000-unit target before further debt is taken on. That leaves the loan available for later working-capital needs.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to ZSR's retained profit, loan and breakage data.

questions.question_text: ZSR is launching its recyclable-glass solar roof tiles. Consider national television advertising, social media and influencer campaigns, or partnerships with housebuilders and installers. Which should ZSR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television: TV would reach millions of households and quickly build awareness of solar roof tiles, useful for a brand seeking growth. However, most viewers cannot install the product themselves and the campaign is expensive for a 36-employee firm funding a $640,000 line. With a 9-day installation lead time, TV awareness that does not reach the housebuilders and installers who fit the tiles is unlikely to convert into the 36,000-unit volume ZSR needs.

Social media and influencers: These can show the recyclable-glass design cheaply and target eco-conscious homeowners, supporting the 61% who would pay $2.00 more. Engagement is measurable and fast. Yet awareness among householders still depends on installers to specify and fit the tiles, so without a channel partner the 66% interest in simpler installation may not become orders, and cost per converted sale could be high.

Housebuilder and installer partnerships: Working through housebuilders and installers reaches the people who actually specify and fit solar roof tiles, exactly where the 450 surveyed homeowners' concerns about installation can be resolved. Partners can demonstrate the 1.4% pilot breakage and the $2.00 eco premium at the point of decision, generating steady volume with modest marketing cost, though agreements take time to negotiate and give partners some bargaining power over price.

Recommendation: ZSR should choose housebuilder and installer partnerships. They convert the 66% and 61% survey signals into real sales and solve the installation concern that TV and social media cannot. Television is rejected as costly and untargeted, and influencers are rejected as awareness without a fitting channel; ZSR should use cheap social content to support the partner-led strategy.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with little ZSR context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to ZSR's market and installation issue.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why television and influencers are rejected.

questions.question_text: ZSR uses a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for ZSR of this approach in reducing the 3.1% tile breakage rate.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A flat structure brings the workforce of 36 close to Sofia Zephyr, so technicians can flag breakage problems on the laminator as soon as they occur and improvements can be agreed without layers of management. That fast feedback helped the pilot reach 1.4% breakage, and quick communication is vital when a lamination setting begins cracking recyclable-glass tiles.

Point 2: Laissez-faire leadership gives skilled technicians freedom to experiment with handling and packing methods, which can generate practical solutions to the 3.1% breakage and the lengthening 9-day installation lead time. Greater autonomy can raise job satisfaction and retention among a small specialist team, protecting the $35.00 selling price and $20.00 variable cost from scrap losses while the $640,000 line beds in, provided clear quality standards are still agreed.

Since the workforce is only 36, one technician's improvement can be shared across the whole line quickly, helping bring the lengthening 9-day installation lead time under control as well as the 3.1% breakage.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to ZSR's breakage, lead time and structure.

questions.question_text: ZSR must train 9 of its 36 technicians on the new laminator. Consider on-the-job training or external certification at $950 per person. Which should ZSR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the laminator is tailored to ZSR's own recyclable-glass process, costs no fees and keeps all 9 technicians productive while they learn, protecting output of 36,000 tiles. The trainer can pass on the exact settings that produced the 1.4% pilot breakage, so improvements are immediate. The weaknesses are the absence of a recognised certificate, which may matter when 61% of homeowners pay more for certified recyclable-glass tiles, and the loss of a senior technician's time while coaching.

External certification: Courses at $950 for 9 staff cost 9 × $950 = $8,550, affordable against the $640,000 investment, and provide a formal credential that supports the 61% premium signal. Outside expertise could also tackle the 3.1% breakage faster. However, 9 of 36 technicians are away from the line, slowing output and lengthening the already 9-day installation lead time, and a generic course may not cover ZSR's exact lamination settings, so some on-site follow-up remains necessary.

Decision: ZSR should choose on-the-job training as the primary method. It is cheaper, specific to the laminator, keeps the 9 staff producing and directly transfers the 1.4% breakage practice into full production at a critical time. External certification is rejected as the main option because the $8,550 and lost capacity would worsen the 9-day lead time for little machine-specific gain; ZSR should add short external certification later if housebuilders require formal proof.

Avoiding the $8,550 also leaves cash to speed deliveries, which matters while the 9-day lead time is a stated problem and the $216,000 fixed costs must be covered from 36,000 units.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with little ZSR application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods applied to ZSR's 9 staff and lead time.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and uses the $8,550 computation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ZSR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $216,000 ÷ ($35.00 − $20.00) = $216,000 ÷ $15.00 = 14,400 units. Answer: break-even output is 14,400 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $35.00 − $20.00 = $15.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $15.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ZSR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 14,400-unit break-even output with actual output of 36,000 units to show a margin of safety of 21,600 units, revealing how far housebuilder orders can fall before the $640,000 line stops covering costs.
2. Use the $15.00 contribution per unit to test the $2.00 eco premium: accepting it lifts contribution to $17.00, so managers can judge whether a small discount to partners still covers the $216,000 fixed costs.
3. Check financing capacity: at 36,000 units ZSR is well above break-even, so managers can test whether the $250,000 bank loan and $140,000 share issue remain serviceable if retrofit spending growth slows to 4.6%.
4. Monitor unit cost of $26.00 ($216,000 ÷ 36,000 units + $20.00) each quarter; a rise would signal that 3.1% breakage is increasing scrap cost and prompt action on the laminator.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 14,400 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $15.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 21,600-unit margin of safety vs 36,000 output; $2.00 premium modelling against $216,000 fixed costs; servicing the $250,000 loan and $140,000 share issue; and $26.00 unit-cost benchmarking to track 3.1% breakage.

working_marks: 1 mark for formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ZSR's profitability. Has ZSR's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 45.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 48.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue rose from $800,000 to $1,000,000 and cost of sales from $440,000 to $520,000, taking gross profit from $360,000 to $480,000. Operating profit increased from $120,000 to $180,000 while capital employed went from $800,000 to $900,000; interest payable was $10,000 then $13,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. Gross margin rose from 45.0% to 48.0%, helped by better control of glass and silicon use as breakage falls from 3.1% toward the 1.4% pilot rate. Operating margin improved from 15.0% to 18.0% because operating profit grew faster than revenue, showing the benefits of spreading fixed costs over more tiles. Returns on capital climbed from 15.0% to 20.0%, so the $640,000 lamination line is already adding profit per dollar employed despite the new loan and share issue. The caution is that eco-building inflation of 7.0% and the 9-day installation lead time could limit sales growth if the 4.6% retrofit expansion stalls, putting the higher margins at risk.

Conclusion: ZSR's profitability has improved: gross margin, operating margin and ROCE all rose together, confirming the investment is paying off. To sustain the 48.0% gross margin and 20.0% return, ZSR should convert the 66% and 61% homeowner interest into housebuilder contracts and press suppliers on the 11.3% glass and silicon increases.

Operating profit grew by $60,000 on $200,000 of extra revenue, so the 48.0% margin reflects both volume and control of the 3.1% breakage; the $900,000 capital employed is plainly being used more effectively.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates margins and returns for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs and capital and a justified conclusion on whether profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ZSR of using recyclable glass and eco-packaging in its solar roof tiles.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recyclable glass and eco-packaging support the premium that 61% of the 450 surveyed homeowners would pay ($2.00 more) and the 66% who would choose solar roof tiles if installation were simpler, protecting the $15.00 contribution per unit. The pilot's 1.4% breakage, versus 3.1% standard, suggests better durability, and the green story helps ZSR differentiate while glass and silicon costs rise 11.3%.

Disadvantage: Recyclable glass and eco-packaging usually cost more than standard materials, which would lift the $20.00 variable cost per unit and require the full $2.00 premium across all 36,000 tiles to avoid squeezing margins. A supply interruption could also push breakage back toward 3.1%, raising scrap and delaying the 9-day installation lead time that already concerns customers.

ZSR must ensure the $2.00 premium is accepted by the 61% of the 450 homeowners through their housebuilders; otherwise the higher material cost cannot be recovered and the $216,000 fixed costs are spread over fewer tiles.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using ZSR's survey, costs and pilot data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in glass and silicon costs will affect ZSR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If ZSR's $250,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage points amount to 0.75% × $250,000 = $1,875 a year (0.0075 × $250,000). This is small next to fixed costs of $216,000 and can be removed by fixing the rate. The secondary worry is that dearer credit may slow the residential retrofit spending that grew 4.6%, reducing housebuilder orders.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.82 an hour): With a workforce of 36, some lamination and packing hours are hourly paid, so wage costs increase and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours or pay rates, so any annual wage figure would be invented; the proper comparison is productivity of 36,000 units ÷ 36 staff = 1,000 units per worker. While that holds, the $15.00 contribution can absorb the rise; if output falls, unit labour cost rises.

Glass and silicon costs (11.3%): These are central to every tile. The $20.00 variable cost is not broken down, so only a labelled bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 11.3%, that adds 11.3% × $20.00 = $2.26 a unit, and across 36,000 tiles about $81,360 a year (36,000 × $2.26). Even a partial pass-through would cut the $15.00 contribution needed to cover $216,000 fixed costs and the $640,000 line, though the $2.00 eco premium offers partial recovery.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in glass and silicon costs will have the greatest impact. It affects every tile, directly erodes the contribution that justifies the laminator, and cannot be neutralised by fixing a loan. The interest effect is small and fixable, and the wage rise can be absorbed at 1,000 units per worker, so both are secondary.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited ZSR application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on ZSR's costs or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
